newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu quits capital for northern palace.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu quits capital for northern palace.

text.p: Zaire's veteran president, Mobutu Sese Seko, fighting cancer and seven months of civil war, left his capital Kinshasa on Friday for his northern jungle palace at Gbadolite on doctors orders, state television said.
But the departure of the man who has dominated Africa's third largest country for over three decades triggered intense speculation that he was on his way into exile.
"The president of the republic went to Gbadolite this morning. He will take a few days of rest on the advice of his doctors," state television reported.

Political and diplomatic sources said earlier that Mobutu's departure followed talks with army chiefs who told him they could not defend the capital against Laurent Kabila's advancing rebel forces and that he should leave for his own safety.
A Western diplomat in Morocco said Mobutu was expected there in the next 48 hours. "It seems that he has chosen Morocco as a place for exile," the diplomat said.
"I am hearing that Morocco is a likely first stop, with France as a final destination," one Western diplomat in Paris said. France declined all comment.
Sources in South Africa, whose president Nelson Mandela has been trying to broker a peaceful handover of power in Zaire, expressed surprise at the developments.
"That's not in line with anything we would have expected to happen on the basis of the information at our disposal," a South African source close to Mandela's negotiating team said.
A close Mobutu relative said that members of Mobutu's entourage were told on Thursday night to pack their bags and be ready to leave Kinshasa by dawn on Friday morning.
There was no immediate comment from Kabila, who was back at rebel headquarters in the southern city of Lubumbashi following talks on Thursday in South Africa with Mandela.
Kabila agreed to a request from Mandela to give Mobutu until Monday to study proposals for a peaceful handover of power.
Asked earlier if he would halt the rebel advance on Kinshasa, Kabila replied: "I have nothing to say about it."
Mobutu, 66, who is reputed to have amassed a huge personal fortune over the years, seized power in 1965. Western powers supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.
The rebels, who took up arms in October demanding Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, now control three-quarters of the impoverished, corruption-plagued country.

Kinshasa, a teeming city of five million people, spent its third night under curfew but a semblance of normality returned on Friday after news that Mobutu was studying the South African peace proposal.
Mobutu had agreed to hand over to an elected successor. Kabila demanded an immediate transfer of power to his alliance.
Mandela has been trying to avert a battle for Kinshasa but many residents are more afraid of a looting rampage by soldiers of Mobutu's notoriously ill-disciplined army.
Many had feared the worst on Thursday, after the collapse on Wednesday of efforts by Mandela to bring Mobutu and Kabila together on a South African ship in Congo.
As reports of Mobutu's departure spread through the streets, opponents expressed cautious satisfaction.
"We are waiting now for Kabila. We hope there has been an agreement to avoid bloodshed," Blaise Bomba, a member of the unofficial opposition "street parliament," said.

Switzerland ordered a freeze on any sale of a Mobutu villa but not all his assets there. The government said the public prosecutor in rebel-held Lubumbashi had requested a freeze of all Mobutu's assets there.
